extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (prosecutors and litigators), in-house counsel, and patent applicants concerned with §101/Alice eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and guidance on applying the Mayo/Alice §101 two-step framework to patent claims, and the differing applications of that framework by the USPTO (MPEP) and by district courts. Focuses on prosecution strategy and how to bridge divergent §101 outcomes between examiners and judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step test (courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two-step Mayo/Alice analysis: Step One — determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (judicial exceptions: law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step Two — if Step One is satisfied, consider the elements of each claim individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application; Step Two searches for an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to 'significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply only these two steps. Courts have rarely found inventive concepts at Step Two, so Step One typically controls the inquiry. Citations: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank; Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP §2106 Alice framework (Step 2A / Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP §2106 implements the Alice analysis as Step 2A (which corresponds to courts' Step One) and Step 2B (which corresponds to courts' Step Two), but subdivides Step 2A into two prongs (Prong One and Prong Two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flow: Step 2A Prong One — determine whether the claim recites a patent-ineligible concept; if yes, Step 2A Prong Two — determine whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application; if not integrated at Prong Two, proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identify judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: At Prong One of Step 2A, examiners determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corresponds to the courts' Step One: is the claim directed to a patent-ineligible concept?

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a 'practical application'
rubrics_metrics.description: At Prong Two of Step 2A, examiners determine whether claims that recite a judicial exception nonetheless recite additional elements that 'integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.' If the exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim is deemed not directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP/2019 Guidance instructs that examiners should evaluate integration into a practical application and, if integrated, may deem claims patent-eligible without proceeding to Step 2B. Prong Two thus incorporates aspects of what courts treat as the Step Two inventive-concept inquiry into Step One analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: How examiners evaluate 'integration into a practical application' (2019 Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners evaluate integration by: (a) identifying any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (b) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application, using one or more of the considerations laid out by the Supreme Court and the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2019 Guidance specifically instructs that 'revised Step 2A specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.' Examiners should give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional, when evaluating whether a judicial exception has been integrated into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept and conventionality analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B corresponds to the court's Step Two: determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to 'significantly more than' the ineligible concept itself. Analysis at Step 2B includes consideration of whether additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Prong Two of Step 2A does not establish integration into a practical application, examiners move to Step 2B to analyze inventive concept and conventionality. The 2019 Guidance reserves conventionality analysis for Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility (MPEP §2106.06(b)) — improvement to technology/computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO allows a 'streamlined eligibility' analysis when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident, e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality, an examiner may find it qualifies as eligible subject matter under §101 without further analysis. This offers a path for quicker allowance where improvements to technology are clear from the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP: transformation may be found at Prong Two or Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP states that for 'a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must “transform the nature of the claim” into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, integration into a practical application (Prong Two) or an inventive-concept finding at Step 2B can both suffice to make a claim patent-eligible under the USPTO framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2024 AI Guidance — reiteration of Step 2A Prong Two approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 Guidance for AI inventions 'doubled down' on asking 'whether the claimed invention as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application,' and reiterates that 'at Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the exception is not integrated into a practical application or that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the exception unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in Step 2B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The updated guidance applies specifically to AI-related claims but underscores the same structural difference: examiners may find integration at Prong Two and need not require evidence unless conventionality is asserted at Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court practice and non-deference to PTO §101 determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts apply the two-step Alice test and have in some cases declined to give weight or deference to the Patent Office's determinations that claims 'integrate' an abstract idea into a practical application. Courts may not expressly use the 'integration into a practical application' language in Step One and instead treat practical-application arguments as part of Step Two inventive-concept analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aviation Capital Partners v. SH Advisors — claims allowed by an examiner under 'integrated practical application' were treated as abstract by a district court, which stated it gave 'no weight to the Patent Office’s overall determination that the patent was eligible.' The Federal Circuit and district courts are not bound by USPTO guidance; case law controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution strategies to bridge USPTO–court divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants facing §101 rejections may consider strategies that account for both MPEP/USPTO guidance and how district courts approach Alice, including creating a record that additional elements are not routine and conventional and pursuing claims of varying scope within the same patent family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested actions: provide analysis beyond USPTO Step 2A Prong Two (e.g., record evidence or arguments that additional elements are not well-understood, routine, conventional); claim drafting to include multiple claim scopes; create a prosecution record useful in later litigation. These strategies may help claims withstand rigorous §101 scrutiny in district court.
